summary: Argues that the Data Transfer and File Transfer Protocols could be revised and simplified based on implementation experience, TIP capabilities and Datacomputer needs. It suggests specific changes to prompt discussion at the upcoming workshop.

eli5.summary: After trying the file rules in practice, the author suggests ways to make them simpler and more useful.

questions: another look at data and file transfer protocols
what is the data transfer protocol
early ftp problems for tip users
subtitle: Proposed simplifications to the Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol, based on early implementation experience.

tldr.problem: Implementing the Data Transfer Protocol (DTP) and File Transfer Protocol (FTP) showed they were hard for TIP users, awkward for the Datacomputer and remote job service, and lacking error recovery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC suggests dropping DTP's transparent mode, making ASCII acceptable, using printable ASCII commands in FTP, adding a restart command, and letting user and server agree on data type, structure and mode.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion paper written to prepare the forthcoming Data and File Transfer Workshop. It updates RFC 264 and RFC 265, and its status is listed as Unknown.

today: The RFC's status is listed as Unknown and no RFC obsoletes it. It updates RFC 264 and RFC 265, and records the early debate on how to simplify DTP and FTP before the planned workshop.

sections.title: Experience So Far
sections.content:
The author reviews ad hoc ways of moving files over the ARPANET. The TENEX CPYNET system connects through the Initial Connection Protocol to server socket 7, sends control information such as user name, password, command and file name, then reopens a new connection with a chosen byte size to carry the file. End of file is signalled by closing the connection. It is efficient because data is not reformatted and the PDP-10 works best with a 36 bit byte size.

Elsewhere, files go through a modified user TELNET, as with the send.file and script features at MIT-DMCG. Transfer rates to most TELNET receiving processes were between 200 and 2,000 bits per second, against 2,000 to 20,000 bits per second NCP-to-NCP.
sections.eli5: People had already found quick ways to send files, and the fastest ones picked the best chunk size for each computer.

sections.title: What Other Users Need
sections.content:
TIPs will not support DTP in its present form, so TIP users find DTP-based services inconvenient. The author suggests allowing ASCII within DTP and using printable ASCII strings instead of numeric codes for commands. TIP users might also want to send data to a specified socket, for example to a line printer, card reader or magnetic tape.

The Datacomputer people at CCA want a single full-duplex connection for control information in Datalanguage, and FTP commands that are printable ASCII. Remote Job Service needs Network ASCII as the default data type and a way to propose and reject other types and structures. FTP also has no way to restart a transmission after a failure.
sections.eli5: Small terminals and special computers found the rules awkward, so the author lists what each of them needs.

sections.title: Proposed Changes to DTP and FTP
sections.content:
For DTP, the author suggests removing the transparent mode, leaving block mode and the indefinite bit-stream mode, and making the "modes available" handshake optional. A simplified DTP might be only a format procedure, with choice of mode, error control, recovery and aborts left to the higher-level protocol. Letting the transfer mode set the byte size, data type and structure is also suggested.

For FTP, the author proposes ASCII commands so a user can talk to a server directly, separate or reopened connections with a suitable byte size, and an NCP interrupt along with close to mark a definite end of file. For restart, the author suggests a command to say where retransmission should begin, such as the SPF command of UCSB's Simple-Minded File System, plus an agreement step for data type, structure and mode.
sections.eli5: The suggestions boil down to this: use plain typed words for commands, let the two computers agree on how to send the data, and allow restarting after a failure.

sections.title: Open Questions
sections.content:
The author asks whether error control belongs in DTP or a higher level, and says this needs further discussion. Block mode is criticized as heavy overhead for just marking end of file and separating data from control information, while using separate connections brings a different overhead.

The concluding remarks hope this discussion will help produce revised specifications that satisfy the diverse needs elegantly.
sections.eli5: The author does not claim to have the final answer, only a list of ideas for a meeting to argue about.
